item.title: Bipartite Carrier Compression and Machine-Certified Bounds in Sch\"onhage Trilinear Multiplication Tensors
item.description: arXiv:2610.14263v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under the conditional framework breaking the longstanding O(n log n) integer multiplication barrier (originating from OpenAI Preprint #109), the asymptotic time complexity exponent T(n) = O(n (log n)^{1-\kappa}) is governed by bounding the second moment E[X^2] < 1 of recursive branching processes over trilinear tensor carrier graphs. In this work, we present a constructive combinatorial optimization over the alternating carrier bipartite matching graphs of the Sch\"onhage trilinear tensor decomposition at dimensions h=23 and h=25. Through an alternating augmenting path search, we uncover a non-trivial cluster-unlocking cascade that eliminates 185 carrier roles (95 roles in h=23 and 90 roles in h=25), reducing the global physical wire width by 377,890 wires from the reviewed baseline W = 177,284,805 down to W = 176,906,915. Evaluated over the exact 10^{-14} rational grid, this wire reduction certifies an improved second-moment coefficient AB = 5,164,059 / 125,000,000,000 and establishes the sharpened conditional exponent \kappa = 826,215,307 / 20,000,000,000,000 \approx 4.131076535 \times 10^{-5}, strictly surpassing the preceding record on this architecture (\kappa \approx 4.123864 \times 10^{-5}). All 47 polynomial constraints and 7 rational security margins are audited in exact Q-arithmetic with zero floating-point error, and the fundamental wire reduction identity is formally verified in the Lean 4 interactive theorem prover without unproven axioms.
item.dc:creator: Volkan Da\u{g}l{\i}, Zerrin Da\u{g}l{\i}, Da\u{g}han Da\u{g}l{\i}

item.title: Constant-Loss Round-Preserving Direct Sums for Information Complexity
item.description: arXiv:2610.15377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strong direct-sum theorems relate the information needed to solve many independent instances of a communication problem to the information needed for one instance. For Gap-Majority composition, an optimal information bound was previously known, but preserving the number of communication rounds incurred an additional logarithmic loss. We prove a round-preserving Gap-Majority lemma with constant additive information loss, independent of both the number of instances and the number of rounds. More generally, we establish a variance direct-sum theorem for additive square-integrable observables over product distributions. For protocols with a bounded number of terminal answer values, the extracted single-coordinate protocols preserve the round budget, and their average information cost is at most the original information cost divided by the number of coordinates, plus a term depending only on the answer alphabet and the allowed variance loss. The proof uses centered counterfactual conditional means and a global variance amortization argument. Rather than encoding absolute conditional means for every possible terminal answer, we encode the information not already determined by the common view. The total squared innovation is controlled by a telescoping variance potential, yielding an information loss independent of the number of coordinates. We also derive same-round mean-square estimation bounds for arbitrary terminal outputs.
item.dc:creator: Haoran Wang

item.title: Execution-Time Opacity in (Controllable) Timed Automata is Hard
item.description: arXiv:2610.15478v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Timing information leakage occurs whenever an attacker successfully deduces confidential internal information by observing some timed information such as the total duration of a run. Timed automata (TAs) are an extension of finite-state automata with a set of clocks evolving at the same rate and that can be tested or reset. Hence, this formalism is able to represent systems involving timing constraints reacting to the passage of time. Some of the transitions in a timed automaton may be controlled, i.e., enabled or disabled, to limit the runs that are allowed. Execution-time opacity (ET-opacity) aims at studying timing information leakage through the analysis of timed automata. More precisely, the ET-opacity problem consists in deciding whether an attacker can deduce whether some secret locations were visited by a run, solely from the run's duration. When control is allowed, the goal becomes to find a strategy that blocks the runs leaking information. This problem has been shown decidable for TAs, with and without control. However, these existing results only provide upper bounds on the complexity of the ET-opacity problem, sometimes largely above the tight bound. Our main contribution is to provide tight lower bounds for those two results. Moreover, for controllable TAs, two variants of ET-opacity (depending on whether detecting if a run did not visit a secret location represents an information leakage or not, and named full and weak ET-opacity respectively) had been separately studied; we prove here that these two notions are inter-reducible.
item.dc:creator: Sarah D\'epernet (Universit\'e de Lorraine, CNRS, Inria, LORIA, Nancy, France), Engel Lefaucheux (Universit\'e de Lorraine, CNRS, Inria, LORIA, Nancy, France)

item.title: Unconditional Separation between LL and CLL
item.description: arXiv:2610.15554v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Catalytic computation involves the study of Turing machines that are provided an additional catalytic tape (with arbitrary content) that the machine may use while ensuring that the tape contents are restored at the end of the computation. Although it is known that catalytic log-space machines are at least as powerful as non-deterministic log-space (and more), we do not have unconditional asymptotic separations. In this work, we prove an unconditional separation between a deterministic space complexity class and its catalytic counterpart. More precisely, at the doubly logarithmic scale, we show that catalytic Turing machines can provably compute more languages than standard deterministic doubly-logarithmic space machines. The separation is witnessed by the unary language $\mathrm{POW2} = \{1^n : n \text{ is a power of two}\}$. We construct a catalytic Turing machine that uses $O(\log \log n)$ bits of space and $O(\log n)$ bits of catalytic tape to decide $\mathrm{POW2}$, whereas any standard deterministic Turing machine requires $\Omega(\log n)$ space to decide it.
item.dc:creator: Shubham Bhardwaj

item.title: Saving the Queen is hard: Hive is EXPTIME-complete
item.description: arXiv:2610.15654v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hive is a boardless two-player strategy game in which the pieces form the playing surface. We prove that deciding whether White can force a win in single-Queen $n$-Hive, the generalization with exactly one Queen Bee per player, is EXPTIME-complete, even when all pieces are already placed. Our hardness proof reduces from unbounded two-player Constraint Logic: Grasshoppers encode edge orientations, while the One Hive rule enforces the vertex constraints. We obtain the EXPTIME upper bound by considering positions up to translation. The result answers the single-Queen question raised by Andel and Rin. Keeping the same inventory and movement rules, it also gives EXPTIME-completeness for multi-Queen variants. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first use of unbounded two-player Constraint Logic to prove EXPTIME-completeness for a natural problem.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Carboni, Daniele Muscillo

item.title: A simplified proof of polynomial improvements for 3SUM and APSP
item.description: arXiv:2610.15663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a simplified proof of the polynomial improvements for integer 3SUM and all-pairs shortest paths (APSP) established by Alman and Vassilevska Williams, with weaker exponents. The central ingredient is selected-entry matrix multiplication: computing a prescribed set of entries of a product of dense rectangular matrices. Starting from Sch\"onhage's inner/outer-product identity, we construct a multiplication rule that shares intermediate products among many outputs. We apply this rule recursively and bound the work by counting the requested entries at each level. Applied to incidence matrices, the algorithm solves Offline Set Disjointness over a small universe. Known deterministic reductions then yield truly subquadratic integer 3SUM and truly subcubic APSP for polynomially bounded integer inputs.
item.dc:creator: Sankeerth Rao Karingula, Shachar Lovett

item.title: NP-hardness of additive approximation for generalized Tur\'{a}n problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.16358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a fixed graph $T$ and a fixed nonempty family $\mathcal{F}$ of graphs, let $\operatorname{ex}(G, T, \mathcal{F})$ denote the maximum number of copies of $T$ in an $\mathcal{F}$-free subgraph of a graph $G$. Alon and Shikhelman~[Algorithmica, 2022] conjectured that if $e(T)> 0$ and no member of $\mathcal{F}$ is a subgraph of a blow-up of $T$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$, approximating $\operatorname{ex}(G, T, \mathcal{F})$ within an additive error $n^{v(T)-\varepsilon}$ is NP-hard for an input graph $G$ on $n$ vertices. The previously established general cases for this conjecture include $\operatorname{ex}(G, K_2, \mathcal{F})$ by Alon, Shapira and Sudakov~[Ann. of Math., 2009], and $\operatorname{ex}(G, K_m, K_k)$ by Alon and Shikhelman. In this paper, we confirm this conjecture for every bipartite graph $T$ and every clique $T$. Our reductions use iterative leaf additions, symmetric rooted extensions and random transversals to encode the maximum number of edges in a $(k-1)$-colorable subgraph of $G$, where $k=\min_{F\in \mathcal{F}}\chi(F)$.
item.dc:creator: Yihan Chen, Jialin He, Xihe Li, Jie Ma, Tianying Xie

item.title: Graph determination problem from knowledge of its subgraphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.16497v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the context of graph reconstruction studies, this paper addresses the problem defined as follows: given a sample of vertex-coloured graphs, each associated with a number, does there exist a connected graph containing exactly the given number of induced subgraphs isomorphic to each graph in the sample, such that every edge of the solution graph is included in at least one of these subgraphs. This paper first shows that this problem is $\Sigma$______-complete. The associated optimisation problem is to determine the minimum number of vertices in a solution graph, if one exists. For instances consisting of two paths, we prove NP-completeness in general and give a polynomial-time dynamic programming algorithm when one path is monochromatic.
item.dc:creator: Coralie Zens (DAVID), Dominique Barth (DAVID), Dimitri Watel (CEDRIC, ENSIIE), Marc-Antoine Weisser (GALaC)

item.title: Learning, Compression, and Meta-Complexity
item.description: arXiv:2610.16535v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The idea that learning is closely tied to compression has long served as both a powerful principle and, at times, an informal analogy across machine learning and learning theory. Here we focus on settings in which that intuition can be made mathematically precise, surveying formal connections among learning algorithms, data compression, and computational complexity theory, with an emphasis on recent progress and current frontiers. We describe how techniques from complexity theory can guide the design of both supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms with provable guarantees, and conversely, how learning algorithms can yield new insights and results in complexity theory. A central theme is the role of data compression as a bridge between learning and complexity, especially through an area called meta-complexity, which studies the computational difficulty of compression problems and time-bounded variants of Kolmogorov complexity.
item.dc:creator: Halley Goldberg, Mikito Nanashima, Igor C. Oliveira

item.title: PSPACE-completeness of the Hunters and Rabbit game
item.description: arXiv:2610.18537v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the Hunters and Rabbit game, hunters shoot at a set of vertices at each round, while an invisible rabbit must move along an edge. We prove that deciding whether a given number of hunters can guarantee capture is PSPACE-complete, even on simple bipartite graphs. The reduction uses intersection nonemptiness for inverse finite automata: one common word must put all automata in accepting states simultaneously. A clique acting as a safe haven and two families of guards force every winning strategy to simulate common transitions. Existing transformations remove the restriction on the rabbit's initial positions and yield PSPACE-completeness for the directed game with one hunter, even on oriented graphs with positive minimum outdegree. Adjusting the guard sizes also proves PSPACE-completeness of the firefighting game, in which the rabbit may remain at its current vertex.
item.dc:creator: Walid Ben-Ameur, Alessandro Maddaloni

item.title: Coarse-Graining Recursive Expert Computation: Continuation-Relative Interfaces and Failure Modes
item.description: arXiv:2610.14413v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Computational coarse-graining aims to replace a sequence of updates with a cheaper module while preserving task performance. We present a continuation-relative evaluation framework that assesses replacements through the computation that follows them, using downstream task quality and total execution cost as joint criteria. The framework distinguishes boundary representations, summaries of skipped computation, executed operations, and downstream loss. It makes interfaces and permitted deployment information explicit, combines fine-path references with directly trained controls using the same shortened architecture, and accounts for selection overhead. An exact loss decomposition separates replacement effects at a fixed downstream action from effects of changing that action. A finite construction shows how retained information can reduce the stipulated cost of zero-error prediction under fixed information and controller restrictions. Experiments in two frozen pretrained language models show that representation fidelity and task loss can favor different fitting objectives. In a prespecified comparison on a 1.7-billion-parameter model, next-token-loss training lowers in-distribution negative log-likelihood by 0.1901 nats per scored token compared with reconstructing the skipped blocks' output, using the same optimizer and update count. This ranking reverses in all nine paired comparisons under distribution shift. In a recursive expert prototype, the jointly adapted candidate lowers task error relative to frozen-bank and router-only baselines, but trails directly trained controls, and the tested input-only selectors fail the joint quality-cost criteria. Together, the protocol and studies provide explicit criteria and diagnostics for distinguishing useful computational replacement from local approximation gains within specified interfaces and evaluation settings.
item.dc:creator: Shihua Yu, Yanzhi Wang, Tianchi Chen

item.title: A Fixed Parameter Sublinear Time Approximation Scheme for Metric Min-Sum Clustering
item.description: arXiv:2610.15148v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Metric $k$-minsum clustering is a simple, natural, appealing density-based clustering criterion whose computational complexity remains poorly understood, despite the progress achieved fornother clustering criteria in the past three decades. In this paper we give an efficient approximation scheme for this problem that runs in sublinear time for mildly increasing $k$, and thus is fixed parameter tractable with respect to the parameter $k$. We complement this result by showing that similar algorithms are unlikely to exist for the closely related problems $k$-median and balanced $k$-median, assuming popular fine-grained complexity conjectures. Specifically, we show that no sublinear time algorithm with small approximation factors can exist even for $2$-median and balanced $2$-median. It was previously known that no efficient PTAS can exist for $k$-median and our results show a strong and perhaps surprising separation between the $k$-minsum clustering problem and $k$-median even in the sublinear regime. Our upper bounds improve qualitatively upon decades old results. Our lower bounds establish the first use of the Distributed PCP framework to clustering problems.
item.dc:creator: Karthik C. S., Euiwoong Lee, Yuval Rabani, Chris Schwiegelshohn, Samson Zhou

item.title: Capturing Bisimulation-Invariant Exponential-Space Complexity Classes
item.description: arXiv:2610.15475v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Otto's Theorem characterises the bisimulation-invariant PTIME queries over graphs as exactly those that can be formulated in the polyadic mu-calculus. This extends to a characterisation of the full bisimulation-invariant exponential-time hierarchy, using a higher-order extension of the polyadic mu-calculus, called PHFL, which is naturally stratified by type order. The bisimulation-invariant fragment of k-EXPTIME is captured by the fragment of PHFL whose formulas have type order at most k. This is obtained using a generalisation of the Immerman-Vardi Theorem by Freire and Martins. Here we provide such a characterisation of the exponential-space hierarchy. We show that the bisimulation-invariant fragment of k-EXPSPACE is captured by the fragment of PHFL of type order k+1 whose formulas are tail-recursive. Tail recursion limits the interplay between fixpoints and higher-order functions so that model checking based on fixpoint iteration can be made more space efficient in a way comparable to tail recursion in programming languages. The capturing result makes use of a generalisation of Vardi's characterisation of PSPACE as first-order logic with partial fixpoints, namely that k-EXPSPACE is captured by higher-order logic of order k+1 with partial fixpoints.
item.dc:creator: Florian Bruse (TU Munich, Munich, Germany), David Kronenberger (University of Kassel, Kassel, Germany), Martin Lange (University of Kassel, Kassel, Germany)

item.title: Lasso Games
item.description: arXiv:2610.15480v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study games on finite graphs with labelled or weighted edges in which plays end as soon as the first loop is formed. The resulting play has a lasso shape: a path (head) followed by a cycle (loop). We consider two semantics for determining the winner: the loop semantics, where only the loop matters, and the lasso semantics, where the entire play is taken into account. We show that adopting the lasso semantics may have a dramatic impact on both the complexity of the game and the memory required to play optimally. Mean-payoff games with lasso semantics are no longer positionally determined, and the threshold problem â€“ deciding whether the value of the game is at least 0 â€“ is PSPACE-complete. In contrast, lasso parity games are equivalent to weak parity games, remain positionally determined and are solvable in polynomial time. Furthermore, we show that if a positionally determined winning objective is closed under cyclic permutation and both the objective and its complement are closed under concatenation, then it is equivalent to the parity objective. Finally, we consider mod-k games, where the winner depends on the length of the path modulo k >= 2. We show that these games, in both semantics, are PSPACE-complete. Alongside computational complexity, we analyze the memory required to play optimally. We establish that for any game positionally determined in loop semantics, memory of size 2^n is sufficient in lasso semantics. We complement this by showing exponential memory lower bounds for lasso mean-payoff and mod-k games.
item.dc:creator: Krzysztof \.Zyndul (University of Warsaw)

item.title: Superpolynomial Lists for Reed-Solomon Codes over Binary Extension Fields
item.description: arXiv:2610.15815v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent work shows that ordinary Reed--Solomon codes over prime fields admit polynomial-size lists up to list-decoding capacity on every evaluation set. We show a contrasting phenomenon over binary extension fields. For every fixed rate $0<R<1$, there exists $\varepsilon_R>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $h$, the full-field Reed--Solomon code over $\mathbb{F}_{2^h}$ has a received word with $n^{\Omega_R(\log n)}$ codewords within relative distance $1-R-\varepsilon_R$. To our knowledge, these are the first superpolynomial ordinary Reed--Solomon list-size lower bounds at fixed positive rate and a fixed positive agreement gap above the rate. Thus capacity-approaching polynomial list size for Reed--Solomon codes is not uniform over the underlying field, and the obstruction occurs at every fixed rate. As a puncturing consequence, the same holds for primitive Reed--Solomon codes; the obstruction is also robust under controlled dense puncturing. The proof begins with an exact correspondence that turns certain binary Bose--Chaudhuri--Hocquenghem weight-enumerator coefficients into sizes of single Reed--Solomon lists. A classical binary weight family gives the initial quarter-rate construction, while a quadratic-form enumeration supplies its superpolynomial multiplicity. A common-kernel quotient/descent argument and common-root padding then extend the construction to all rates. We also determine the optimized agreement envelope achieved by the construction.
item.dc:creator: Minshen Zhu

item.title: Two Linear Programs are Better than One
item.description: arXiv:2610.15909v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The extension complexity $\operatorname{xc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$ is the minimum number of facets of a polytope that projects onto it. Motivated by the complexity of neural networks, Hertrich and Loho introduced the virtual extension complexity $\operatorname{vxc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$, which is the minimum of $\operatorname{xc}(Q) + \operatorname{xc}(R)$ among all polytopes $Q$ and $R$ such that $P+Q=R$. We show the following results pertaining to virtual extension complexity. First, we resolve the core open problem on the topic by showing the virtual extension complexity can be exponentially smaller than extension complexity. Second, we show there are matroid base polytopes with exponential virtual extension complexity by adapting a semi-algebraic counting argument by Hrube\v{s} that extends the counting arguments of Rothvoss. Finally, we show that the maximum virtual extension complexity of a polygon with $n$ vertices is $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$. This resolves an analogue of a question on extension complexity of Fiorini, Rothvoss, and Tiwary in 2011 in the case of virtual extension complexity.
item.dc:creator: Alexander E. Black, Christoph Hertrich, Stefan Kober, Georg Loho

item.title: Bootstrapping Classical and Quantum Query Lower Bounds for Finding Tarski Fixed Points
item.description: arXiv:2610.16209v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Tarski fixed-point problem asks for a fixed point of a monotone map on a $k$-dimensional grid lattice of width $n$ and has applications in game theory, economics, and verification. Substantial gaps remain between the known upper and lower bounds on its quantum query complexity. We prove two hardness bootstrapping theorems for quantum query lower bounds. Starting from a hard instance family whose instances have pair-wise incomparable unique fixed points, and a lower bound established by the nonnegative adversary method, we bootstrap this lower bound by (i) a factor of $\Omega(t)$ when the dimension is multiplied by $t$ and the width remains unchanged, and (ii) a factor of $\Omega(\log m)$ when the width is multiplied by $m$ and the dimension is doubled. Applying these theorems, we obtain three consequences: (i) an $\Omega(k\log^2 n)$ lower bound for $k\geq 4$, improving previously best-known classical and quantum lower bounds; (ii) for every fixed constant $\alpha>0$, there exists a constant $\delta(\alpha)>0$ such that $Q_\epsilon(\text{Tarski}(n,k))=\Omega(kn^{\delta(\alpha)})$ whenever $k>n^\alpha$, and in particular, an $\Omega(kn^{0.0072})$ lower bound for $k>n^{2/203}$, the first lower bound with simultaneous linear dependence on the dimension and polynomial dependence on the width; and (iii) a superpolynomial lower bound of $(k/\log k)^{\Omega(\log k)}$ for exponentially wide grids, where $n=2^{\Theta(k)}$. The last result rules out a route to polynomial-time algorithms for simple stochastic games and ARRIVAL through generic polynomial-query black-box Tarski solvers.
item.dc:creator: Tongyang Li, Weiran Ma, Ziyi Yang, Xingyu Zhao

item.title: Period Piece: NEXPTIME-complete problems on digraphs via Boolean network dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.16561v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The central object in this work is the Boolean network, a function $f:\{0,1\}^V \to \{0,1\}^V$. Often identified with $f$ is its dynamics $D_f$, the digraph with exactly $\{x \to y : f(x)=y\}$ as its arcs. The interaction graph of $f$ is the digraph $G$ on $V$ which can be thought of as representing the dependencies of the components of $f$ on one another. On the other hand, model-checking is a major field of study in graph algorithms and complexity. We consider problems at the intersection of these paradigms: for a given property $\phi$, we say that a digraph $G$ is $\phi$-dynamic if $G$ is the interaction graph of some Boolean network $f$ such that $D_f \models \phi$. The corresponding decision problem $\phi$-DYNAMIC asks whether $G$ is $\phi$-dynamic. Problems of this form are well-studied in the Boolean networks community. For example, it is a well-known result that, letting $\phi$ be 'No fixed points' (i.e. $\nexists x:x\to x$), $\phi$-DYNAMIC is equivalent to the structural digraph problem NON-ACYCLIC, which is solvable in linear time. We establish, for the first time, properties $\phi$ for which $\phi$-DYNAMIC is computationally hard. These include the 'Unique fixed point' property $\exists!x:x\to x$, and a range of properties concerning the periodic points of $f$ (i.e. vertices of $D_f$ which lie on a cycle). More widely, we exhibit an infinite family of natural properties $\phi$ such that $\phi$-DYNAMIC is $\mathrm{NEXPTIME}$-complete, which we call PERIOD PIECE. As a special case, these include all properties of the form 'Unique cycle of length $k$' and 'Exactly $k$ fixed points' for any $k \ge 1$. On the other hand, we show that if the input digraph has bounded in-degree, then for those same problems $\phi$-DYNAMIC collapses down to $\mathrm{NP}^{\mathrm{NP}}$, the second level of the polynomial hierarchy, though it remains $\mathrm{NP}^{\mathrm{NP}}$-complete.
item.dc:creator: Florian Bridoux, Maximilien Gadouleau, David C. Kutner, Adrien Richard

item.title: Graph Distortion Distances, Gromov-Hausdorff and the Hardness of Gromov-Wasserstein
item.description: arXiv:2610.16926v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the computational complexity of graph distortion distances, a family of graph metrics measuring how vertex distances differ between two graphs. Formally, these distances are defined in terms of standard matrix norms on the difference of distance matrices under an optimal vertex alignment. The resulting metrics have natural interpretations, corresponding to three ways of measuring the distortion of shortest-path distances: the maximum distortion among all vertex pairs (entrywise maximum norm), global aggregation (entrywise $p$-norms), and local aggregation (operator $p$-norms) of distortions. For maximum distortion, we show that approximation below a factor of two is NP-hard even for highly restricted trees. Due to the close connection to the Gromov-Hausdorff distance, we obtain a similar hardness result for the latter. In both cases, we show essentially optimal additive inapproximability. On the algorithmic side, we give a subcubic-time algorithm for optimal embeddings of connected graphs into paths, based on a structural decomposition along a diametral path. Additionally, we give a simple approximation algorithm when one input graph has a "relatively path-like" metric structure, i.e. has bounded pathlength. For local and global distortion, we derive various hardness results even for restricted inputs. Making use of a close connection between the global distortion distances and Gromov-Wasserstein distances, we give the first formal proof of NP-hardness of the latter, which has been claimed in the literature many times but has, to the best of our knowledge, never been correctly proven.
item.dc:creator: Jens Breitung, Timo Gervens, Julius P\"orzgen

item.title: Sensitivity of Rotation Symmetric Boolean Functions via Binary Necklaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.17006v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rotation symmetric Boolean functions are Boolean functions invariant under cyclic permutation of their variables and can be represented by binary necklaces. We express local sensitivity as a weighted bichromatic degree in the necklace quotient and derive an exact formula for the multiplicities between neighboring necklaces. For an odd prime number of variables, we obtain explicit sensitivity formulas and show that multiplicity corrections occur only on an asymptotically negligible family of necklaces. For monomial rotation symmetric Boolean functions, we prove that every odd-degree function has maximum sensitivity, determine the sensitivity of every quadratic function, and determine the sensitivity of the consecutive quartic family. We also determine exactly the sensitivity of cyclic run-threshold functions for arbitrary length and threshold.
item.dc:creator: Yuan Li, Jing Zhang

item.title: Block Sensitivity and Certificate Complexity of Rotation Symmetric Boolean Functions
item.description: arXiv:2610.17100v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study block sensitivity and certificate complexity of rotation symmetric Boolean functions, with particular emphasis on monomial rotation symmetric Boolean functions. We first show that every odd-degree monomial rotation symmetric Boolean function on $n$ variables satisfies $s=bs=C=n$. We then determine sensitivity, block sensitivity, and certificate complexity for every quadratic monomial rotation symmetric Boolean function. For the quadratic function $Q_{n,k}$ generated by $x_0x_k$, we prove, outside the short-orbit case, that \[ C(Q_{n,k})= \begin{cases} n,&4\mid n/\gcd(n,k),\\ n-\gcd(n,k),&4\nmid n/\gcd(n,k). \end{cases} \] Moreover, \(bs(Q_{n,k})=C(Q_{n,k})\) for every quadratic MRS function, and outside the short-orbit case, strict separation \(s<bs=C\) occurs exactly when \[ \frac{n}{\gcd(n,k)}\equiv2\pmod4. \] Finally, for the consecutive quartic family \[ R_n(x)=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z_n}x_ix_{i+1}x_{i+2}x_{i+3}, \] we determine all three measures in every residue class modulo $6$, using the sensitivity formulas and, in one residue class, finite-state results established in our companion preprint~\cite{LiZhangRSBFSensitivity}. In particular, for $r=2,3$ and $6q+r\ge5$ we obtain strict separation, \[ \boxed{s(R_{6q+r})=6q<bs(R_{6q+r})=C(R_{6q+r})=6q+1,\qquad r=2,3.} \] Thus this family gives an infinite collection of rotation symmetric Boolean functions for which sensitivity is strictly smaller than block sensitivity, while block sensitivity and certificate complexity coincide.
item.dc:creator: Yuan Li, Jing Zhang

item.title: Query Complexity of Densest Sub(hyper)graph Problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.17581v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rubinstein et al. introduce the study of connectivity and minimum cut problems in the cut query model, where an algorithm can only access the edges of a graph through CUT queries. In this work, we examine the query complexity of densest subgraph problems. Our first contribution is to generalize the uniform sparsification approach for Densest Subgraph and other heavy subgraph problems to weighted graphs, achieving the following results. >A $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted Densest Subgraph in $O(n\log^2 n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, roughly matching the $\Omega(n/\log n)$ lower bound we prove for randomized algorithms. >A $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted Max Cut in $O(n\log^2 n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries. This improves upon the bound of $O(n\log^3 n(\log n+1/\varepsilon^2))$ queries achieved by Plevrakis et al., making significant progress towards their lower bound of $\Omega(n/\log n)$ queries. In contrast, we rule out approximation schemes with truly subquadratic query complexity for Densest $k$-Subgraph and settle its exact query complexity in both the unweighted and deterministic settings. For hypergraphs, we show CUT queries alone cannot achieve $o(\sqrt{n})$-approximation for Densest Subhypergraph or $o(n)$-approximation for Densest $k$-Subhypergraph, regardless of the number of queries. Augmenting CUT queries with the EDGE oracle of Chen et al., we overcome this barrier for Densest Subhypergraph and obtain a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation on rank-$r$ hypergraphs using $O(nr\log n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries. We also extend our Densest $k$-Subgraph hardness results to hypergraphs and prove exponential query lower bounds for exact Densest $k$-Subhypergraph. Lastly, confirming a conjecture of Chakrabarty and Liao, we show that simulating an ADD query using CUT and IS-EDGE$^?$ queries requires exponentially-many queries.
item.dc:creator: Sinan G. Aksoy, Eli Friedman, Nate Veldt, Stephen J. Young

item.title: Nearly Optimal Quantum Sample Complexity of Learning Fourier-Sparse Boolean Functions
item.description: arXiv:2610.17648v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the number of uniform quantum examples needed to exactly learn a Boolean function with at most $k$ nonzero Fourier coefficients. We give a learner with near-optimal $\widetilde{O}(k)$ sample complexity independent of the input length $n$. The learner uses only separate measurements of individual examples. This improves the previous $O(k^{3/2}\log^2 k)$ upper bound (Arunachalam, Chakraborty, Lee, Paraashar, and de Wolf, 2021). The main ingredient is a candidate set formed by symmetric differences of subsets from independent groups of Fourier samples. A multilinear majority polynomial combines unbiased random approximations into an accurate witness whose Fourier support lies in this set. Granularity then forces the set to contain the entire Fourier support, including subsets never directly sampled. For comparison, we derive the tight classical sample complexity $\Theta(nk)$ by combining known sparse-recovery and lower-bound results.
item.dc:creator: Zekun Ye

item.title: Hitting Minors: Stronger Lower Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2610.17664v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For a fixed finite collection of graphs $\mathcal{F}$, the $\mathcal{F}$-Minor-Free Deletion problem asks, given a graph $G$ and an integer $k$, whether there is a set $S\subseteq V(G)$ with $|S|\leq k$ such that $G-S$ contains no graph of $\mathcal{F}$ as a minor. This generalizes Vertex Cover, Feedback Vertex Set, and Vertex Planarization, among many others. Baste, Sau, and Thilikos [JCSS 2020, SICOMP 2023] showed that, assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), there are collections $\mathcal{F}$ for which the problem cannot be solved in time $2^{o(\mathrm{tw}\log\mathrm{tw})}n^{O(1)}$ on $n$-vertex graphs of treewidth $\mathrm{tw}$, and gave a matching algorithm. We ask whether this super-exponential dependence persists under more restrictive structural parameters. First, we strengthen their lower bound. Assuming ETH, for every fixed $h\geq 6$, $\{P_h\}$-Minor-Free Deletion, where $P_h$ is the path on $h$ vertices, cannot be solved in time $2^{o(t\log t)}n^{O(1)}$, where $t=\mathrm{fvs}+\mathrm{td}$ is the sum of the feedback vertex set number and treedepth of the input graph. These two parameters are incomparable, but both individually upper bound the treewidth. Together with the $2^{O(\mathrm{tw}\log\mathrm{tw})}n^{O(1)}$-time algorithm of Baste, Sau, and Thilikos [SICOMP 2023], our lower bound is tight. In contrast, we show that asymptotically faster algorithms are possible when parameterized by the vertex cover number $\mathrm{vc}$. Specifically, for any finite family $\mathcal{F}$, $\mathcal{F}$-Minor-Free Deletion can be solved in time $2^{O(\mathrm{vc})}n^{O(1)}$. Taken together, our results show that the boundary between single-exponential and super-exponential complexity for this problem lies between the vertex cover number and the feedback vertex set number (plus treedepth).
item.dc:creator: Jongseo Lee, Roohani Sharma, Sebastian Wiederrecht

item.title: Path Length Existence Problems in Bounded-Treewidth Probabilistic Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.17887v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider the problem of computing the probability of existence of a source-to-target path or walk satisfying a given length constraint in an input probabilistic graph. The length constraints we consider can require the length to be at least $\ell$, at most $\ell$, or exactly $\ell$, for $\ell$ a target length given as input. The probabilistic graphs that we consider are directed graphs where each edge is annotated with an independent probability of existence. As this task is generally intractable (#P-hard), we aim for algorithms applying to input graphs that are assumed to be of bounded treewidth. We classify the complexity landscape of these problems: - We give an XP algorithm parameterised by treewidth to compute the probability that an input probabilistic graph contains a source-to-target path/walk of length $\geq \ell$, and do the same for a path/walk of length $\leq \ell$. - We show that the four problems mentioned in the last item are W[1]-hard parameterised by pathwidth (hence not FPT under the standard assumption that FPT$\neq$W[1]). This is in contrast to the case of non-probabilistic graphs, where the corresponding problems were known to be FPT parameterised by treewidth; and to the connectivity problem (and more generally MSO evaluation) on probabilistic graphs, where the same was known. - Surprisingly, we show that it is #P-hard to compute the probability that an input graph contains a source-to-target path/walk of length exactly $\ell$, even on graphs of pathwidth $2$. By contrast, all our problems are tractable on graphs of treewidth $1$. - Last, we investigate the complexity of our problems when the edges can carry weights. This causes all our problems to become #P-hard already on pathwidth-2 graphs, and causes specifically the ``exactly $\ell$'' walk problem to be #P-hard even on pathwidth-1 graphs.
item.dc:creator: Antoine Amarilli, Mika\"el Monet, Harshul Sagar

item.title: Solving SAT via Treewidth Backdoors in Linear Time: Beyond Sparsity
item.description: arXiv:2610.18540v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) problem is a remarkably expressive computational problem, serving both as a cornerstone of complexity theory and as a unifying language for a wide range of search and reasoning tasks. While $\mathrm{NP}$-complete in general, SAT is well known to be linear-time solvable on instances with bounded treewidth. This motivates the search for "hidden" tree-like structures in formulas---for instance by detecting so-called weak $t$-treewidth backdoors. Such backdoors are sets of $k$ variables that can be assigned in such a way that the remaining instance has treewidth at most $t$ and is satisfiable whenever the original instance is. Ever since Gaspers and Szeider [ICALP 2012] showed that finding a weak $t$-treewidth backdoor for a SAT formula is $\mathrm{W}[2]$-hard with respect to $k$, tractability results have been restricted to structurally sparse formulas---most notably, a linear-time algorithm for $d$-SAT (bounded clause-length SAT) by Fomin, Lokshtanov, Misra, Ramanujan, and Saurabh [SODA 2015] and a non-uniform polynomial-time algorithm when the incidence graph of the input formula belongs to a nowhere-dense graph class (or more generally is $K_{d,d}$-free) by Lokshtanov, Panolan, and Ramanujan [ICALP 2022]. In this paper, we push the tractability boundaries of finding weak $t$-treewidth backdoors beyond sparsity and into the regime of "well-behaved" dense formulas. Aiming towards relaxing structural input restrictions from nowhere-dense to edge-stable graph classes, as featured in the theory of beyond sparsity for FO model checking, or to bounded VC-dimension set systems, we identify signed semi-ladder-freeness as the correct dense structural restriction that establishes the boundary between tractability and intractability along this line.
item.dc:creator: Jan Dreier, Robert Ganian, Marlene Gr\"undel, Roohani Sharma, Simon Wietheger

item.title: $T$-efficient unitary synthesis via block-sparse Hamiltonian simulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.18589v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We construct Clifford+$T$ circuits implementing arbitrary $n$-qubit unitaries with worst-case $T$-count $\widetilde{O}(N^{8/7})$ at constant operator-norm error, where $N=2^n$, improving the previous exponent $5/4$. The construction uses $\widetilde{O}(N^{6/7})$ clean ancillas. The main idea is to reduce the data addressed by each query to the block-encoding circuit for a sparse piece while controlling the additional simulation work needed to combine the pieces. We simulate a Hermitian logarithm of the target by flattening its traceless part with a two-layer random similarity transformation, randomly partitioning the transformed generator into block-sparse Hermitian pieces, and combining their evolutions using qDRIFT. For a target operator-norm error $\epsilon\in(0,1/2)$, let $L=\log_2(N/\epsilon)$, the qubit count plus the requested bits of accuracy. By successively correcting the approximation error, we obtain a circuit using $\widetilde{O}(N^{8/7}L^{3/7}+NL)$ $T$ gates and $\widetilde{O}(N)$ clean ancillas whenever $L\le N$. We also prove that, at constant precision, the exponent $8/7$ is optimal within a sequential block-SELECT model.
item.dc:creator: Diyi Liu, Shuchen Zhu, Wibe Albert de Jong, Di Fang, David Williams-Young, Chao Yang

item.title: CLS Hardness of 2D Min-Max Optimization with Product Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2610.18678v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the complexity of computing approximate first-order Nash equilibria in min-max optimization problems with one dimensional min and max players and product constraints. For black-box access to the objective, we prove that any algorithm requires $\Omega(1/\sqrt{\epsilon})$ queries to find an $\epsilon$-first-order Nash point. In the white-box setting, we establish CLS-hardness by reducing from End-of-Potential-Line. These results show that even the simplest min-max setting with one dimensional min and max players is at least as hard as CLS and therefore does not admit polynomial-time algorithms unless $\mathsf{CLS}\subseteq \mathsf{P}$.
item.dc:creator: Alkis Kalavasis, Panagiotis Patsilinakos, Stratis Skoulakis, Manolis Zampetakis

item.title: On Collusion-Free Teaching in Planar Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.18714v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Non-clashing teaching minimizes teaching complexity among models satisfying the Goldman--Mathias collusion-avoidance criterion. While the Vapnik--Chervonenkis dimension (VCdim) measures the complexity of learning from samples, non-clashing teaching dimension (NCTD) measures the number of examples required when a teacher can select them. Whether NCTD is always bounded above by VCdim remains a fundamental open question in learning theory. In this paper, we investigate this question for the concept classes of closed neighborhoods in planar graphs. We prove a tight upper bound of two on their NCTD, thereby establishing the conjectured inequality for this family. For the positive variant NCTD+, in which teaching sets contain only positive examples, we obtain a tight upper bound of four. Finally, we show that deciding whether either NCTD+ or NCTD is at most one is NP-complete, even for concept classes of closed neighborhoods in planar graphs. In particular, despite the upper bound of two on NCTD for such classes, distinguishing between NCTD values of one and two remains NP-hard.
item.dc:creator: Khazaliya Liana, Kuske Clemens

item.title: Exploring Minimal Blocking Sets for Kernelization Lower Bounds for $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion
item.description: arXiv:2610.18719v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For Vertex Cover, a minimal blocking set of a graph $G$ is an inclusion-wise minimal vertex set contained in no minimum vertex cover of $G$. Bougeret et al. [SIDMA 2022] showed that, for all minor-closed graph classes $\mathcal{G}$, Vertex Cover has a polynomial kernel parameterized by the distance to $\mathcal{G}$ if and only if $\mathcal{G}$ has bounded minimal blocking sets. In this work, we explore how far this connection between minimal blocking sets and kernelization extends to $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion parameterized by the deletion distance to $\mathcal{G}$. A minimal $\mathcal{F}$-blocking set of $G$ is a minimal vertex set not contained in any optimal $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion solution of $G$. For connected families $\mathcal{F}$, we show that if some graph class $\mathcal{G}$ closed under disjoint union has unbounded minimal $\mathcal{F}$-blocking sets, then $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion parameterized by the deletion distance to $\mathcal{G}$ has no polynomial kernel. This generalizes a result of Hols et al. [SIDMA 2022] for Vertex Cover. We then show that this criterion does not capture all kernelization lower bounds for $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion, even for minor-closed graph classes. Motivated by the work of Dekker and Jansen [Discrete Appl. Math. 2024], we study the more general notion of extended $\mathcal{F}$-blocking sets and the kernelization lower bounds they yield. For every fixed integer $\eta\geq 1$, Pw-$\eta$ Deletion is the problem of deleting at most $k$ vertices to reduce the pathwidth to at most $\eta$. We show that it has no polynomial kernel parameterized by the distance to graphs with pathwidth at most $\eta+1$. Moreover, for connected families $\mathcal{F}$, we show that $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion parameterized by the distance to graphs with pathwidth at most $\max_{F\in\mathcal{F}} pw(F)+1$ has no polynomial kernel.
item.dc:creator: Ahmed Ghazy, Jakob Greilhuber, Tim A. Hartmann

item.title: Bipartite Matching with Few Rounds of Demand Queries
item.description: arXiv:2610.18777v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the randomised and deterministic demand-query complexity of approximate bipartite matching with few query rounds. The demand-query model, introduced in [Blumrosen and Nisan SICOMP 2009; Nisan SODA 2021], is inspired by combinatorial auctions and welfare maximisation, where an oracle returns the first neighbouring vertex (item) of a vertex u (agent) according to a given permutation pi (preference ordering of the agent over the items). For randomised algorithms, our main result gives a trade-off between the number of rounds k, the per-round query budget q=n^{1+\delta}, and the achievable approximation ratio. Let 1 <= k <= log n, and -1 <= delta <= 1/k. Every k-round randomised algorithm using O(q) demand queries per round has a worst-case expected-size approximation factor of Omega(n^{1/2k-delta/2}/k). Conversely, we give a randomised algorithm achieving approximation factor O(n^{(1-k*delta)/(k+1)}/k) in expectation. For deterministic algorithms, for k*q >= n, we show that the optimal deterministic approximation factor is ~Theta(n^2/(q*k^2)), thereby improving the previous lower bound of [Nisan SODA 2021] by a polynomial factor over a wide range of parameters. In particular, for q=Theta(n), we improve the deterministic round-complexity lower bound for constant-factor approximation from ~Omega(n^{1/3}) to ~Omega(sqrt n). Our algorithms produce matching and vertex-cover certificates; the deterministic trade-off also extends to minimum vertex cover and maximum fractional matching. We extend the randomised upper bounds to the weaker Demand-OR model [Nisan 2021]. We prove a non-adaptive simulation of uniform random-neighbour queries using known techniques, avoiding the O(log n)-round penalty of the trivial binary-search simulation. Consequently, our upper bounds yield the same k-round approximation guarantees using O(q * log^2 n) Demand-OR queries per round.
item.dc:creator: Shravan Mehra, Sagnik Mukhopadhyay, Vihan Shah

item.title: The Polynomial Hierarchy does not collapse
item.description: arXiv:2405.18439v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The arithmetical hierarchy (AH) is similar to the polynomial hierarchy (PH). Unlike the PH, the AH does not collapse relative to any oracle. A $\Sigma_{k+1}$-complete language is computably enumerable (c.e.) relative to the k-th level of the AH. So, given an oracle in the k-th level of the AH, we require exhaustive search to recognize whether the input string is in the language. We can define a language in AH with a quantified formula and a computable relation. The encoding lengths of the bounded variables are unbounded. However, if we observe only finitely many input strings, then there exist integers such that the encoding lengths of the bounded variables can be limited to these integers without changing the result of the formula for each input string. By adding padding arguments of length equal to those of the bounded variables and padding of length equal to the runtime required to compute the relation, we construct an equivalent language in PH. An OTM operating on the language with padding arguments in PH with a padded oracle has the same program flow as it does on the original language with the unpadded oracle in the AH. The number of oracle queries does not change. We still need brute-force search therefore, the required number of oracle queries is exponential. The PH does not collapse.
item.dc:creator: Reiner Czerwinski

item.title: Optimal Lower Bounds for Symmetric Modular Circuits
item.description: arXiv:2604.04760v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A notorious open question in circuit complexity is whether Boolean operations of arbitrary arity can efficiently be expressed using modular counting gates only. H{\aa}stad's celebrated switching lemma yields exponential lower bounds for the dual problem - realising modular arithmetic with Boolean gates - but, a similar lower bound for modular circuits computing the Boolean AND function has remained elusive for almost 30 years. We solve this problem for the restricted model of symmetric circuits: We consider MOD$_m$-circuits of arbitrary depth, and for an arbitrary modulus $m \in \mathbb{N}$, and obtain subexponential lower bounds for computing the $n$-ary Boolean AND function, under the assumption that the circuits are syntactically symmetric under all permutations of their $n$ input gates. This lower bound is matched precisely by a construction due to (Idziak, Kawa{\l}ek, Krzaczkowski, LICS'22), leading to the surprising conclusion that the optimal symmetric circuit size is already achieved with depth $2$. Motivated by another construction from (LICS'22), which achieves smaller size at the cost of greater depth, we also prove tight size lower bounds for circuits with a more liberal notion of symmetry characterised by a nested block structure on the input variables.
item.dc:creator: Benedikt Pago

item.title: Failure of the strong feasible disjunction property
item.description: arXiv:2604.04830v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A propositional proof system $P$ has the strong feasible disjunction property iff there is a constant $c \geq 1$ such that whenever $P$ admits a size $s$ proof of $\bigvee_i \alpha_i$ with no two $\alpha_i$ sharing an atom then one of $\alpha_i$ has a $P$-proof of size $\le s^c$. We combine the work of Ilango (2025) and Ren et al. (2025) with the gadget proof complexity generator of K. (2007) and rule out the property for strong enough proof systems under the following two hypotheses: - there exists a language in class E that requires exponential size circuits even if they are allowed to query an NP oracle, - there exists a P/poly demi-bit in the sense of Rudich (1997).
item.dc:creator: Jan Krajicek

item.title: On the Hardness of Finding Temporally Connected Subgraphs of Any Size
item.description: arXiv:2604.23226v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Temporal graphs are graphs whose edges are present only at certain points in time. Reachability in these graphs is defined via temporal paths, in which edges are traversed in increasing chronological order. A temporal graph is temporally connected (or TC) if every ordered pair of vertices is connected by a temporal path. When the graph itself is not TC, a natural question is whether it admits a TC subgraph (a.k.a.~closed temporal component) of a given size $k$. This question was one of the earliest and most studied in the field, shown to be NP-hard by Bhadra and Ferreira in 2003. We strengthen this result dramatically, showing that deciding if a temporal graph admits a TC subgraph \emph{of any size} (beyond the trivial case of a single vertex in the directed case and a single edge in the undirected case) is already NP-hard. Our result holds for all standard temporal graph settings, answering a series of open questions in the field and strengthening several existing results. This sharply separates closed components from open ones (where temporal paths can travel outside the component), for which the analogous problem is trivially solvable in polynomial time. As a by-product, our reductions imply that the size of the largest TC subgraph cannot even be approximated within a factor of~$(1-\epsilon)n$ in directed graphs, and within a factor of~$(1-\epsilon)\frac{n}{2}$ in undirected graphs. They also complete the complexity landscape for TC subgraphs of size exactly $k$ when parameterized by $k$ (answering the missing ``non-strict'' case). Our results also have structural implications. In particular, they imply that there exist arbitrarily large TC graphs without nontrivial TC subgraphs, and that there exist TC graphs of arbitrary girth, both facts being of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: Arnaud Casteigts, Christian Komusiewicz, Nils Morawietz

item.title: Hardness Conjectures as Information Constraints: Does Complexity Theory Need New Axioms?
item.description: arXiv:2606.04257v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove that no length-optimal propositional proof system exists if and only if every sound theory $\mathcal S{\supseteq}S^1_2$ with polynomial-time decidable axioms fails to simulate $S^1_2{+}\mathsf{Exp}{+}\phi_{BB}(k)$ for all sufficiently large $k$, where $\phi_{BB}(k)$ asserts the exact $k$-state Busy Beaver value and $\mathsf{Exp}$ asserts total binary exponentiation. Thus a widely believed proof-complexity conjecture admits an information-constraint formulation in terms of Busy Beaver values. For finitely axiomatized sequential $\mathcal S$, a Kolmogorov Blindness conjecture predicts exponential proof-length lower bounds for true randomness extensions, even after adjoining another true randomness axiom if the target remains random conditional on the added string. We also show that a separate hierarchy-level information constraint implies noncollapse of the polynomial hierarchy. These information constraints parallel known results: Liu--Pass characterize one-way functions by average-case hardness of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity $K^t$; Allender et al. relate $KT$ complexity to circuit size up to polynomial factors; Ball et al. characterize key agreement and one-way functions using one interactive problem with different gap parameters. We propose a research program to unify these connections through precise constraints on proof size, average-case time, and circuit size, and ask whether a common framework could justify a new axiom schema for complexity theory. Independence from $ZFC$ remains open. Unconditionally, for each fixed sound $\mathcal S$, any fixed sound computably axiomatized certifying theory extending $EA$ certifies simulation of only finitely many randomness extensions of $\mathcal S$. Defining efficiency as provable efficiency in a fixed theory relocates this difficulty.
item.dc:creator: Hunter Monroe

item.title: A fully Lean-verified quadratic lower bound on the border determinantal complexity of $x_1^n+\cdots+x_n^n$ over $\mathbb{C}$, including the symmetric and exact models
item.description: arXiv:2606.13628v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present the first end-to-end Lean-verified superlinear lower bound on border determinantal complexity. Let $F_n=x_1^n+\cdots+x_n^n$. We prove, over $\mathbb{C}$, that the border determinantal complexity of $F_n$ is at least $(n-1)^2/(4e)$ and its symmetric border determinantal complexity is at least $(n-1)^2/(2e)$; the same bounds therefore hold for exact determinantal complexity. Together with known $O(n^2)$ constructions, both border quantities are $\Theta(n^2)$. The proof compares one enumerative invariant on two sides of a degeneration. On the determinant side, the $(n-2)$nd multidegree of the multiplicity-one Gauss graph of any size-$m$ affine-linear determinant is bounded by an explicit multihomogeneous B\'ezout number; no smoothness, irreducibility, or squarefreeness is assumed. On the target side, a flat limit of these effective Gauss-graph cycles contains the conormal variety of the projective Fermat cone, whose relevant multidegree is the classical dual degree $n(n-1)^{n-2}$. Effectivity gives the inequality in the correct direction, and an $(n-1)$st root yields the quadratic bound. All four bounds are fully verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib. The Lean theorems assume only $n\ge 3$ and a literal determinantal representation or literal border membership, and depend on no axioms beyond Lean's foundational ones. The formal proof follows a localized version of the argument presented here: where the text compares global cycles, it compares local intersection lengths of finite slices of those cycles. Lean sources: https://github.com/karthik202321/power-sum-dc-lean; archived release: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23274251
item.dc:creator: Karthik Sheshadri

item.title: New lower bounds on tensor rank of $(n,2,m)$ matrix multiplication with GPT-6
item.description: arXiv:2609.14393v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The tensor rank of $n\times 2$-with-$2\times m$ matrix multiplication is at least $\left\lceil \frac{24m+2}{5} \right\rceil$ if $m\ge n=3$ and at least $(n+2)m+n-3$ if $m\ge n\ge 4$, over arbitrary fields. This result matches the Hopcroft-Kerr upper bound for $n=3$ and $m\le 6$.
item.dc:creator: Jason Yang

item.title: Exponential Correlation Bounds for Polynomials
item.description: arXiv:2609.28839v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove that the XOR of $k$ majorities on disjoint blocks of $\ell$ bits has correlation at most $(4d/\sqrt{\ell})^k$ with every Boolean-valued degree-$d$ polynomial over an arbitrary field. By known techniques, we obtain explicit pseudorandom generators that fool such polynomials on $n$ Boolean inputs with seed length $d^2\cdot\polylog(n/\varepsilon)$. The correlation and the generator extend to small $\mathsf{AC}^0[q]$ circuits, for every fixed prime power $q$. These results resolve several long-standing questions in circuit complexity and pseudorandomness.
item.dc:creator: Eshan Chattopadhyay, Pooya Hatami, Chin Ho Lee, Shachar Lovett, Avishay Tal, Emanuele Viola

item.title: W[1]-Hardness of Upper Clique Transversal
item.description: arXiv:2610.04917v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A clique transversal of a graph is a set of vertices intersecting every maximal clique. We prove that deciding whether a graph has an inclusion-wise minimal clique transversal of size at least $k$ is W[1]-hard when parameterized by $k$.
item.dc:creator: J. Pascal Gollin, Tesshu Hanaka, Ekkehard K\"ohler, Martin Milani\v{c}, Yushi Uno

item.title: On the Computational Complexity of Problems: Formalizing Sensitivity to Uncertainty and Parametric Complexity Classes
item.description: arXiv:2610.05385v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Worst-case analysis, the setting of the $P \stackrel{?}{=} NP$ question, measures the cost of a problem as a function of input size alone. Yet problems that are exponential in general often become polynomial, even linear, once a checkable property of the input is known: Partition, for instance, is decidable in linear time on inputs whose elements are all equal. We develop a framework that makes such knowledge an explicit parameter $K$ of complexity statements. Costs are measured for fixed algorithms; we distinguish the promise cost from the guarded cost that also pays for checking $K$, and introduce the residual uncertainty $\Psi(n,K)$, the number of input cells that, together with $K$, determine the input. An Uncertainty Reduction Theorem decomposes the guarded cost into checking $K$, locating and reading the residual information, and solving an explicit reduced problem. The classes $P_\upsilon[K]$ and $NP_\upsilon[K]$ are restrictions to polynomial-time promises, made informative by the coverage of $K$. We show that small $\Psi$ forces sparsity but not tractability, characterize FPT as uniform membership in graded families $P_\upsilon[K_k]$, prove a free-variable threshold for SAT, and show that under the factoring assumption no checkable property of non-negligible coverage makes factoring easy. We relate the framework to promise problems, kernelization, average- and generic-case complexity and beyond-worst-case analysis, illustrate it on Partition, Graph Isomorphism, SAT, Vertex Cover and TSP, and apply it to guarded algorithm dispatch with latency contracts and optimal guard ordering, to solver routing in agentic AI, and to the role of promises in quantum speedups.
item.dc:creator: Yannis Tzitzikas

item.title: Broadcasting under Structural Restrictions
item.description: arXiv:2504.13669v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In the Telephone Broadcast problem we are given a graph $G=(V,E)$ with a designated source vertex $s\in V$. Our goal is to transmit a message, which is initially known only to $s$, to all vertices of the graph by using a process where in each round an informed vertex may transmit the message to one of its uninformed neighbors. The optimization objective is to minimize the number of rounds. Following up on several recent works, we investigate the structurally parameterized complexity of Telephone Broadcast. In particular, we first strengthen existing NP-hardness results by showing that the problem remains NP-complete on graphs of bounded tree-depth and also on cactus graphs which are one vertex deletion away from being path forests. Motivated by this (severe) hardness, we study several other parameterizations of the problem and obtain FPT algorithms parameterized by vertex integrity (generalizing a recent FPT algorithm parameterized by vertex cover by Fomin, Fraigniaud, and Golovach [TCS 2024]) and by distance to clique, as well as FPT approximation algorithms parameterized by clique-cover and cluster vertex deletion. Furthermore, we obtain structural results that relate the length of the optimal broadcast protocol of a graph $G$ with its pathwidth and tree-depth. By presenting a substantial improvement over the best previously known bound for pathwidth (Aminian, Kamali, Seyed-Javadi, and Sumedha [ICALP 2025]) we exponentially improve the approximation ratio achievable in polynomial time on graphs of bounded pathwidth from $\mathcal{O}(4^\mathrm{pw})$ to $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{pw})$.
item.dc:creator: Yudai Egami, Tatsuya Gima, Tesshu Hanaka, Yasuaki Kobayashi, Michael Lampis, Valia Mitsou, Edouard Nemery, Yota Otachi, Manolis Vasilakis, Daniel Vaz

item.title: On the (In)Approximability of the Monitoring Edge Geodetic Set Problem
item.description: arXiv:2507.00708v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The minimum \emph{Monitoring Edge-Geodetic Set} problem asks for a minimum vertex subset $M$ such that for every edge $e$ of the input graph $G$, there exist a two vertices $u,v \in M$, that monitor $e$, i.e. every shortest path between $u$ and $v$ in $G$ contains $e$. We prove that this problem cannot be approximated within an $\Omega(\log n)$ ratio in polynomial time unless $\mathsf{NP} \subseteq \mathsf{ZTIME}(n^{O(\log \log n)})$. Additionally, we establish hardness and conditional running-time lower bounds for exact algorithms on $2$-degenerate, $3$-degenerate, and $1$-apex $2$-degenerate graphs. Moreover, we design an approximation algorithm for hereditary graph classes with efficiently computable, truly sublinear-size balanced separators. This achieves an $O(n^{\frac{1}{4}} \sqrt{\log n})$ approximation ratio for $K_h$-minor-free graphs ($h=O(1)$), bounded genus graphs, and $k$-apex graphs ($k=O(n^{\frac{1}{4}})$). For graphs with bounded treewidth, the algorithm yields an $O(\log^{3/2} n)$ approximation ratio.
item.dc:creator: Davide Bil\`o, Giordano Colli, Luca Forlizzi, Stefano Leucci

item.title: The Serial Scaling Hypothesis
item.description: arXiv:2507.12549v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While machine learning has advanced through massive parallelization, we identify a critical blind spot: some problems are fundamentally sequential. These "inherently serial" problems-from mathematical reasoning to physical simulations to sequential decision-making-require sequentially dependent computational steps that cannot be efficiently parallelized. We formalize this distinction in complexity theory, and demonstrate that current parallel-centric architectures face fundamental limitations on such tasks. Then, we show for first time that diffusion models despite their sequential nature are incapable of solving inherently serial problems. We argue that recognizing the serial nature of computation holds profound implications on machine learning, model design, and hardware development.
item.dc:creator: Yuxi Liu, Konpat Preechakul, Kananart Kuwaranancharoen, Yutong Bai

item.title: Parameterized Capacitated Vertex Cover Revisited
item.description: arXiv:2604.18746v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Capacitated Vertex Cover is a generalization of Vertex Cover where we seek a set of $k$ vertices covering all edges, but with the added constraint that for each vertex we are given a capacity, that is, a maximum number of incident edges the vertex can cover if selected. This problem is well-studied in parameterized complexity and is known to be in XP but W[1]-hard parameterized by treewidth. Natural dynamic programs lead to complexities of the form $C^{\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{tw})}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$, $\Delta^{\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{tw})}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$, or $k^{\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{tw})}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$, where $C, \Delta$ are respectively the maximum capacity and maximum degree. These results imply an FPT algorithm for parameter $k$ with complexity $k^{\mathcal{O}(k)}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$, as $\mathrm{tw}\le k$. These simple dynamic programming algorithms essentially constitute the state of the art. Our main question is therefore whether these algorithms can be improved. We address this question from numerous angles...

item.title: Elfs, transducers and quantum walks
item.description: arXiv:2605.30013v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Electric flow sampling (elfs) is a new tool in the quantum walk toolbox and a useful primitive for solving search, sampling and optimization problems on graphs. We refine this tool by showing that there exists a zero-error transducer for implementing elfs. More broadly, we establish a zero-error transducer for reflecting about the intersection of two subspaces, yielding an errorfree transducer version of the effective gap lemma. Building on this result, we obtain improved quantum walk algorithms for estimating effective resistances and span program witness sizes with an optimal error scaling, and for sampling from the random walk arrival distribution, via the composition of many elfs. Using this last algorithm, we obtain an up-to-quadratic quantum speedup for semi-supervised learning on expander graphs.

item.title: Polynomial Binary Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2607.08908v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In a binary polynomial optimization problem (BPO, in short) we are maximizing a multilinear polynomial expression depending on n binary variables. This is a hard optimization class, containing many NP-hard problems, including unconstrained quadratic binary optimization. Several tractable special classes were considered in the literature, including problems with bounded tree-width (Crama, Hansen, Jaumard, 1990), Berge-acyclic problems (Buchheim, Crama, and Heck, 2019), $\beta$-acyclic problems (Del Pia and Di Gregorio, 2022, 2023), limited reach problems (Clausen, Crama, Lusby, Rodr\'iguez, and Ropke, 2024), and $\alpha$-acyclic problems with bounded rank (Del Pia and Khajavirad, 2025). We focus on a general variable elimination scheme for BPO, and develop the unique explicit multi-linear polynomial form for the equivalent BPO problem obtained after the elimination of a given subset of the variables. The obtained closed form representation of such an equivalent BPO problem allows us to characterize new special classes for which this elimination method, when applied recursively, provides a computationally efficient solution. Our approach is elementary1, algebraic, and provides efficient solution to a wide problem class that properly generalizes all of the above mentioned tractable special cases.

item.title: Tight Approximation Thresholds for Geometric Stabbing
item.description: arXiv:2607.28062v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study geometric covering problems: stabbing axis-parallel squares and cubes by coordinate hyperplanes, stabbing horizontal segments by horizontal and vertical lines, and transversal of separated $d$-intervals. We prove matching NP-hardness bounds for their natural covering-LP thresholds. For every $\varepsilon>0$, square stabbing is NP-hard to approximate within $2-\varepsilon$, horizontal-segment stabbing within $e/(e-1)-\varepsilon$, and, for every fixed $d\ge2$, cube stabbing and separated $d$-interval transversal within $d-\varepsilon$. The results hold with finite candidate sets and when arbitrary admissible lines, hyperplanes, or track points are allowed. We construct harmonic integrality-gap families for squares and cubes and use the Kovaleva--Spieksma gap family for horizontal segments. In each family, every object meets a candidate of every orientation. We lift these gaps through the strict-CSP framework of Kumar, Manokaran, Tulsiani, and Vishnoi, using the Unique Games theorem to obtain NP-hardness. An ordered sampler preserves the LP marginals, coupled shifts make every local sample feasible, and a small perturbation through an absorbing label connects every local support. Cartesian cloning removes rational weights, after which disjoint blocks of candidate coordinates realize each output constraint by one square, cube, or horizontal segment. Applying the same transfer theorem to rectangle-hitting gaps of Pach and Tardos, we prove that stabbing axis-parallel boxes by supplied candidate lines in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is NP-hard to approximate within any fixed constant factor. Incidence-preserving algebraic maps yield the same hardness for hitting boxes in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and halfspaces in $\mathbb{R}^6$ by points from supplied finite candidate sets.

item.title: Constant-round quantum advantage in communication complexity for total functions
item.description: arXiv:2608.19787v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that there exists a total function for which there is a polynomial gap between the randomized and the constant-round quantum communication complexity. Previously, such a separation was known only for quantum protocols using polynomially many rounds.
item.dc:creator: Atsuya Hasegawa, Fran\c{c}ois Le Gall

item.title: Quadratic Word Equations with a Linear Side: Polynomial Nielsen Graph Diameter and NP-Completeness
item.description: arXiv:2609.21785v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The satisfiability problem for word equations asks whether variables can be replaced by words so that the two sides become equal. For regular word equations, in which each variable occurs at most once on each side, satisfiability is NP-complete. For general quadratic word equations, in which each variable occurs at most twice in total, satisfiability is NP-hard, but its membership in NP remains open. We consider an intermediate class: quadratic word equations with a linear side, where each variable occurs at most once on one designated side. We show that the Nielsen graph of an equation $U=V$ in this class, with total length $N=|U|+|V|$, has diameter $O(N^{12})$, measured over reachable pairs of vertices. Together with the known NP-hardness for regular word equations, this result establishes NP-completeness of satisfiability for this class. We also show that each strongly connected component is isomorphic to the length-preserving reachability graph of a regular equation, and that the condensation graph has depth at most $|U|+2|V|$.For arbitrary quadratic word equations, we further show that Nielsen paths can be shortened to a length polynomial in the equation size and the number of prefix operations between variables repeated on opposite sides. This yields NP membership for subclasses defined by variable occurrence arrangements.

item.title: Recognizable Picture Languages: Separating UREC from coUREC via Communication Complexity
item.description: arXiv:2609.26047v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce communication-complexity lifting techniques into the study of recognizable picture languages. As an application, we resolve a long-standing open problem of Anselmo et al. (2006) by constructing a language in UREC whose complement does not belong to REC. Our lower-bound argument is inspired by the communication-complexity approach to unambiguous automata of G\"o\"os et al. (2022), although its implementation in the setting of picture languages requires substantially different technical ingredients.

item.title: QMA(2) with Limited Shared Entanglement
item.description: arXiv:2609.39668v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A $\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ protocol involves two provers submitting unentangled witnesses to a polynomial-time quantum verifier. In The Power of Unentanglement (ToC, 2009), Aaronson et al. proposed $\mathsf{QMA}(2;h)$, a variant of $\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ in which the two provers may share $h$ EPR pairs. Our main result shows that the power of $\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ remains unchanged for up to logarithmically many shared EPR pairs: $\mathsf{QMA}(2;h)=\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ for $h=O(\log n)$, where $n$ is the input length. The result follows from a simulation using four unentangled witnesses, combined with the Harrow-Montanaro equality $\mathsf{QMA}(4)=\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ (FOCS, 2010). We also prove monotonicity in the EPR budget: $\mathsf{QMA}(2;h)\subseteq\mathsf{QMA}(2;H)$ for $h\le H$, preserving completeness and soundness. Combined with input padding, this shows that establishing $\mathsf{QMA}(2;n^\varepsilon)=\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$ would imply equality for every polynomially bounded budget, resolving the open problem raised by Aaronson et al. Finally, we extend these results to a variant of the model in which the provers may use local operations and classical communication (LOCC) during witness preparation. For logarithmic-size witnesses and inverse-polynomial gaps, both models remain equivalent to their unentangled counterpart when $h=O(\log n)$. We show that extending this equivalence to any superlogarithmic EPR budget in the LOCC model would imply $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}$.

item.title: The rank of $3\times 3$ matrix multiplication over $\mathbb{F}_2$ is 23
item.description: arXiv:2610.11823v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rank of the tensor of $3\times 3$ matrix multiplication over the field with two elements is at most $23$ by Laderman's algorithm, and Rudich and Rousseau recently proved that it is at least $22$. We prove that it equals $23$. Hence Laderman's algorithm uses the fewest multiplications among all bilinear algorithms over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and among all bilinear algorithms with integer coefficients. The proof uses the substitution method in the form developed by D'Ambrosio, Wang and Yang et al., which bounds the number of first factors of a decomposition that lie in a given subspace of the space of first factors. We sharpen these bounds for $111$ of Wang's $496$ classes of subspaces, constrain the ranks of the first factors through a $27\times 27$ flattening of the tensor, and list, up to symmetry, all sets of $22$ first factors that satisfy these constraints. An exact completion search shows that none of them is the set of first factors of a decomposition. The computation emits certificates, which are checked in the Lean 4 proof assistant. In one formal proof the largest checks are evaluated as compiled code, and in a second one the kernel evaluates every check, so that its final theorem depends only on the three standard axioms of Lean. The Lean proofs build on the formalization of Rudich and Rousseau and import their table of bounds and their reduction for block algorithms.
